summary: Documents the North American Directory Forum's agreement on how entries are named in the public portions of the North American Directory. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1417.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a naming rulebook for a big directory. A newer version replaced it.

questions: how are entries named in the north american directory
how to name organizations in x500
subtitle: A naming standard for the North American X.500 directory

tldr.problem: X.500 is a directory system that lets you look up people and organizations, but different regions had different conventions for naming entries, making it hard to find things across North America.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC establishes a unified naming scheme for the North American directory that uses the existing civil naming infrastructure: country (US), states, counties, and cities form the hierarchy, with organizations and persons modeled within this structure. Entries can be listed at multiple levels so they can be found in different contexts.
tldr.outcome: The scheme was adopted by the North American Directory Forum and provided a foundation for directory services in the 1990s, though it was later replaced by RFC 1417 as the standard evolved.

today: RFC 1255 is an informational document that defined the X.500 directory naming scheme for North America in 1991. It was replaced by RFC 1417 as the standard evolved.

sections.title: The Need for a Unified Naming Scheme
sections.content:
Computer networks rely on naming and numbering infrastructure, just as the physical world does. For example, network addresses must be assigned carefully to prevent collisions. The X.500 standard defines a Directory Information Tree (DIT)—a hierarchical database where people and organizations can be looked up by name.

However, X.500 is just a technical framework. It does not specify how a particular region should actually name its entries. The North American Directory Forum (NADF) recognized that if every provider used different naming conventions, users would have difficulty finding information across the region.

This RFC documents the NADF's agreement on how entries should be named in the North American (c=US) portion of the X.500 directory. It uses the existing civil naming infrastructure—countries, states, counties, and cities—as the basis for the directory hierarchy, ensuring that the directory structure mirrors real-world administrative divisions that users already understand.
sections.plainLanguage: A phonebook for computers needs rules about how to file names. This explains the rulebook so everyone files things the same way.

sections.title: Rights and Registry: The Foundation
sections.content:
Before an entry can appear in the directory, three stages must occur. First, there must be a right-to-use: some authority must grant the right to use a particular name. Names used publicly are constrained by law (for example, business names are registered with a state or county). This RFC emphasizes that the directory does not grant rights; it assumes names are already rightfully registered through existing civil authorities.

Second, the name must be registered by binding it to an entry's attributes. For example, an organization registers its name with a state, just as people are registered by birth.

Third, the name is published in the directory. Here is the crucial insight: unlike registration (which is a single master record), publication in a directory can be multiple. A single organization might be listed in multiple places in the DIT so that searchers can find it from different angles. For example, a national company might appear under the national level, under each state where it operates, and under counties within those states.
sections.plainLanguage: Before something can go in the phonebook, someone official must say the name is real. Then the organization registers it. Then it can be listed in the book in many places so different people can find it different ways.

sections.title: The Hierarchy: National, Regional, and Local
sections.content:
The directory structure mirrors civil administration. The root object is c=US (country = United States). Under this are two types of regional objects. States and state-equivalents (modeled as stateOrProvinceName) use the Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 5 list of official state names. Each state entry contains its FIPS numeric and alphabetic codes for compatibility.

Also at the national level are ADDMD operators (Administrative Directory Management Domains), which are the public directory service providers themselves. These provide private namespaces for their own organizational information.

Below each state is the local level: counties or county-equivalents, modeled as locality entries named using FIPS 55 (the Federal standard for populated places). This level can further contain specific municipalities or cities listed as additional locality values, aiding in searches for entities in particular towns.

The RFC emphasizes that while this structure is hierarchical, entities can be listed at multiple levels. A national company can appear at the national level, at the state level, and at the county level, making it findable from different starting points in the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is filed like a map: first by country (US), then by state, then by county. A big company can be listed at all three levels so anyone can find it.

sections.title: Organizations and Persons
sections.content:
The RFC defines three levels of standing for organizations. An organization with national-standing is chartered by the US Congress or has a name registered with the ANSI (American National Standards Institute) registry. Regional-standing means the organization is chartered by a state or has a 'doing business as' (DBA) registration with a state. Local-standing means it is chartered or registered at the local (city/county) level.

The standing of an organization determines how its name appears in the distinguished name. For example, a nationally-standing organization appears simply as {c=US, o=Organization Name}, while the same organization listed at the state level appears as {c=US, st=California, o=Organization Name, c=US}. This redundancy of country information distinguishes the national organization from a regional one with the same name but different standing.

Within organizations, entries may include organizational units, roles, persons, devices, and applications, organized as a subtree under the main organization object.

For persons, the RFC distinguishes between organizational persons (employed by an organization) and residential persons (listed by their place of residence). Residential persons are identified by their locality, state, and distinguishing attributes (such as postal code, street address, or a serial number for uniqueness) to ensure no two residents have identical names.
sections.plainLanguage: Big organizations appear at the national level. Smaller ones appear at state or county level. People appear where they live. The naming system figures out where to list things based on their importance and reach.

sections.title: Practical Examples and Scheme Evolution
sections.content:
The RFC includes extensive examples of how organizations and persons are named. A national laboratory has national-standing and appears directly under c=US. A company with a state DBA registration appears under its home state, but may also list under other states where it operates. A small local business appears under its county, distinguished by a FIPS code because the name alone may not be unique within the county.

An international organization (with foreign-standing) includes its home country in the distinguished name, such as {c=US, o=Erik's Fisk, c=SE} to distinguish it from domestic organizations with similar names.

The appendix documents the scheme's evolution through seven revisions before the first published RFC version, showing how the NADF refined the approach. Early versions attempted to use US trademarks (which failed because a trademark can be issued to different companies in different industries) or numeric FIPS codes (unpopular because less meaningful). The final approach uses alphanumeric names derived from official registries, balancing human readability with stability.
sections.plainLanguage: Different examples show how to name a national lab, a state-registered company, a local shop, and a foreign restaurant. The naming rules were refined many times before they worked well.
